title: Rosalind and the Radiators
premise: Mara Eastwick, a translator who has spent a decade in London letting her mother's Hungarian fade from her tongue, returns to the shuttered family house when it goes to auction. Sorting the rooms, she finds photographs of her mother Rosalind with a man Mara never knew existed—her father, perhaps—and letters that recast her childhood silence as something chosen for her, not by her. As bidders circle and her brother pushes to sell quickly, Mara must decide whether to translate the past faithfully or keep softening it as she always has. She ends by buying back one small thing—the radiators' brass valves, absurdly—and speaking a full sentence of Hungarian aloud at the grave, forgiving both her mother and herself.
about_author: Wren Crane is the pen name of a former court interpreter who grew up between two languages and one silence. 'Rosalind and the Radiators' is their first novel, written in a rented flat above a closed auction house.

chapters.title: The Auction Notice
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. A plain envelope arrives: 14 Alder Row goes under the hammer in six weeks. Mara, mid-translation of someone else's grief novel, realizes she hasn't spoken Hungarian aloud since the funeral. Emotional beat: dread disguised as efficiency; she accepts the trip before she can talk herself out of it.

chapters.title: Fourteen Alder Row
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. The house smells of dust and cold iron; the old radiators still knock at dusk like something pacing. Her brother Daniel arrives with skip bags and a valuation app. Emotional beat: the shock of a home rendered into inventory, and Mara's reflexive retreat into tidying rather than feeling.

chapters.title: Borrowed Words
chapters.summary: Flashback chapters alternate: young Mara learning English at school while her mother's Hungarian shrank to endearments and scoldings. Present-day Mara catches herself translating a memory instead of having it. Emotional beat: tenderness sharpened by loss; language as the first inheritance to be spent.

chapters.title: The Stranger in the Photograph
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Behind a radiator panel, wedged where heat once hid it, she finds a photograph: her mother laughing beside an unknown man on a Danube pier, dated two years before Mara's birth. On the back, one word in Hungarian: 'várj' — wait. Emotional beat: vertigo; the past acquires a face.

chapters.title: Daniel's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Daniel's POV. He wants a fast sale; the house is costing them monthly, and his marriage is fraying under the weight. He reads Mara's digging as avoidance. Emotional beat: sympathetic pressure—he isn't wrong about money, only blind to what Mara is actually grieving.

chapters.title: Mrs. Kertész Remembers Everything
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. An elderly neighbor, sharp-tongued and half-blind, recognizes the man in the photo: István, a lodger during the hard winter, deported after a paperwork error no one fought. Rosalind wrote him letters for years. Emotional beat: the relief and cruelty of testimony; Mara learns her mother's silence had architecture.

chapters.title: Letters, Untranslated
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. In the attic trunk: István's replies, which Rosalind kept but apparently never answered—or did she? Mara translates slowly, her rusty Hungarian failing exactly where the letters grow most tender. Emotional beat: rising tension; each page costs her more vocabulary, and time, before the auction.

chapters.title: The Viewing
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. Open-house day: strangers appraise her childhood, Daniel charms a developer, and Mara overhears a couple mock the 'ugly old radiators.' She finds herself defending them in Hungarian before catching it. Emotional beat: climax approaches; invisibility fails publicly, and Mara stops apologizing for it.

chapters.title: What the House Sold For
chapters.summary: Climax. At the auction, bidding climbs beyond Daniel's hopes. Mara, using money meant for nothing else, wins a single lot: the lot of salvaged fixtures—brass radiator valves, the photograph, the letters. Confrontation with Daniel in the car park; grief finally spoken in both languages. Emotional beat: rupture turning toward repair.

chapters.title: Várj
chapters.summary: Mara's POV, coda. She installs one valve on her London radiator, pins the photograph above her desk, and visits Rosalind's grave with flowers and a full sentence of Hungarian, practiced until true. She begins translating István's last letter properly—for herself, not a client. Emotional beat: resolution; forgiveness as an act of translation, imperfect and complete.
